newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonds seen dipping if rate cut too small.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonds seen dipping if rate cut too small.

text.p: Spanish bonds could dip this week if the central bank shaves its money market rate by an expected 25 basis points, seen as too little by the market, dealers and financial analysts said on Monday. If the Bank of Spain does not lower the rate by 50 basis points at Thursday's repurchase tender, the 10-year futures Bono contract which has been rising fast since August could dip by more than a full basis point to the 105 level, they said.
The Bank of Spain has lowered its official rate five times so far this year, cutting it down from nine to 7.25 percent.
The government's 1997 budget draft is seen as one of the most severe Spain has ever passed.
Analysts said the central bank could remain cautious and not trim the rate further before September's consumer price inflation data is out on October 11.
"The market has already discounted a 50 basis point cut," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Madrid's Bank of America.
"But if, as I expect, the Bank of Spain will do less than that, say 25 basis points, the market will push the yields up above eight percent for the 10-year bonds."

Analysts said short dated bonds in particular could be disrupted by disappointment on the official rate. The yield curve could flatten if the Bank of Spain is less generous than expected because the short end will be hit harder.
But dealers said the market was not too bothered.
With a big focus on the Euro convergence, Italian and Spanish bonds saw some panic buying this month, a trend which is likely to continue until the peseta joins the single currency.

In a joint interview with the local financial daily Expansion and the Financial Times published on Monday, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said Spain would do everything needed to be at the starting block of the European Monetary Union.
Traders said foreign investors, who usually bet on the longest part of the curve, were likely to buy on every dip.
"The mood will continue to be positive in the long term," a dealer at Fimat in Madrid said.
